newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO says Hebron deal far off, blames Israel.
newsitem.headline: PLO says Hebron deal far off, blames Israel.

text.p: Palestinian officials say a Hebron agreement with Israel -- which negotiators were saying for two weeks was just around the corner -- is not likely soon.
"Most of the essential points we have not resolved," a senior Palestinian official, who did not want to be identified, told Reuters late on Friday.
Asked if an accord on the West Bank town was far off, the official responded: "Yes."

Both Israeli and Palestinian negotiators had said recently that a deal was near on the long-promised handover to Palestinian rule of 80 percent of the volatile West Bank city of Hebron, where some 400 Jews live among more than 100,000 Arabs.

Israeli officials charged the Palestinians with delaying a Hebron accord. "There is a desire on behalf of the Palestinians to stall and to delay and to drag it on," said David Bar-Illan, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's media adviser.

Jewish settlers sparked new Palestinian anger on Friday when they occupied a West Bank hilltop. The settlers agreed to remove the seven mobile homes from the site on Sunday, in exchange for a meeting the same day with Israeli government officials.

U.S. Middle East special envoy Dennis Ross was due to hold another round of talks with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on Sunday to try to close gaps between the sides. Ross has also held a series of meetings with Netanyahu.

"I think all that is happening shows that the American position is not neutral but in many situations the Americans take the position very close to the Israeli position which makes reaching an agreement difficult," Palestinian Minister Nabil Shaath told Reuters.

"Sometimes the American co-sponsor implies that we are creating new issues, as if we are delaying the negotiations, as if there is a desire not to reach the liberation of Hebron," Shaath said after the weekly cabinet meeting in Gaza on Friday.
In Washington, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns rejected suggestions that the Palestinians were to blame for the failure this week to conclude the Hebron accord.

"It takes two to tango, and both are responsible. So we're not pointing the finger at the Palestinians or at the Israelis and saying that one or the other has more responsibility than the other to make an agreement," Burns told a news briefing.
Shaath said the central issue holding up a deal was Israel's refusal to commit itself to a timetable for futher West Bank pullbacks after Hebron, as stipulated in previous peace deals.

"The main stumbling block is the refusal of the Israeli government and the Israeli negotiating team to accept clearly and in a written form its commitments to withdraw and redeploy its forces in the West Bank," Shaath said.
"We are not going to spend our lives like we did in Hebron negotiating again and again every phase of redeployment in the West Bank."
Israel was to have redeployed its troops in Hebron some 10 months ago under a 1995 interim accord but violence and security concerns have held it up.
Palestinian officials pointed out Friday's settlement bid near PLO-ruled Ramallah was in one of the rural areas Israel was supposed to evacuate in the next stage of the accord.
